THE DESIGN CONCERN RAISED BY THE PROJECT OWNER:

The controller attribute `[RequireRole("Manager","Director")]` on ApprovalsController duplicates role eligibility that is already represented in the `Approval:RoleLimits` configuration section. If a new role (say "VicePresident" with a limit) is added to Approval:RoleLimits, it would have a configured approval limit but still be blocked by the hardcoded controller attribute. This conflicts with the documented convention in AGENTS.md that adding an eligible role should not require editing multiple hardcoded locations.

THE OPTIONS UNDER CONSIDERATION:

A. Status quo — keep the hardcoded attribute. Accept the duplication as defence in depth.
B. Remove the attribute from ApprovalsController entirely; rely solely on ApprovalService/ApprovalPolicy to refuse with reason code RoleCannotApprove (403).
C. Replace it with a marker attribute (e.g. [RequireApprovalAuthority]) whose filter resolves ApprovalPolicy from DI and calls policy.CanApprove(session.Role). Keeps a route-level gate but derives its data from the single source of truth.
D. Adopt the full ASP.NET Core authorization stack (ClaimsPrincipal, authentication handler, AddPolicy/IAuthorizationHandler) driven from the same configuration.

MY CURRENT RECOMMENDATION IS C, with these supporting arguments:
1. Two distinct concerns are being conflated: "can this principal use this endpoint at all" (route-level, cross-cutting) versus "may this person approve THIS invoice at THIS amount given prior approvals and the submitter" (domain). C keeps both layers but gives them one shared source of truth.

AGENTS.md documents that role names compare ignoring case. So a role configured as "manager" would be accepted by the domain but rejected by the attribute.
